newsitem.title: USA: Another week in paradise for stock market investors.
newsitem.headline: Another week in paradise for stock market investors.

text.p: It was another week in paradise for investors as stocks romped into record territory. But the key to the greatest bull market in history will be how corporate earnings stack up.
Stocks again rewrote the history books, with the Dow Jones industrial average scaling new heights and setting four record highs this past week.

Even more impressive, the world's most closely watched stock index, which features 30 of the largest U.S. companies, has racked up eight record closes in the last 12 trading sessions of the New Year, extending a bull market that started six years ago.
On Friday, the Dow was again in new high ground, gaining 67.73 points to close at 6,833.10 and beating Thursday's record close of 6,765.37. For the week, it was up 129.31 points.
The leap in stock prices has been generated by an explosion in corporate profits, which have jumped nearly 140 percent since 1991.
The earnings of the Standard & Poor's 500 companies are estimated to have risen by more than 18 percent last year after an increase of 11.5 percent in 1995.
But analysts say the market is overextended, and there is concern that the earnings growth may drop to single digits, with some predicting an increase of less than 3 percent.
The market is at a major crossroads, the experts say, and earnings for the just completed fourth-quarter of 1996 will be very important in setting the direction of the stock market this year.
The investing public will be looking for the magic of stronger profits in the earnings reporting season that got underway this past week, and how the numbers compare with those of a year earlier.
If the earnings story is good, it should send the market to fresh highs, but if the numbers are disappointing, then the market could be in for a nasty fall.

At this stage of the extended bull market, which has defied gravity, the experts say that investors should start to ask themselves, "How much can they lose rather than 'How much can I make out of this market.'"

They say that even a dartbboard approach to picking stocks has proved to be successful during the market's surge of 60 percent in the last two years and investors have only known the reward side of the equation.
Greg Smith, chief investment strategist for Prudential Securities says that ultimately, it all comes down to corporate earnings.
"Whether you call it excessive exhuberance or a good run based on fundamentals, stock-market strength is a function of investors' perceptions of the profit outlook," he said.
"The profit outlook for 1997 still looks fairly good to me," Smith said, estimating high-single-digit profit growth.

Alan Ackerman, senior vice president and market strategist for Fahnestock & Co. said that corporate earnings are in the "crosshairs" and Wall Street is lowering its sight on this year's earnings growth.

"The market may have reached a near-term saturation point, with stocks having moved up more rapidly than expected and now, many investors are waiting for earnings to match stock performances," he said.

"The market will likely be overly sensitive to disappointments, which will be devastating to some stocks and close comparisons are likely to be somewhat negative but sharply higher numbers should keep some stocks ahead of the pack," Ackerman said.
But others see a difficult year for earnings comparisons.

"A great deal of the growth in earnings in the past few years has come from corporate downsizing such as staff layoffs, which have been one-time productivity increases and actually translate into an accounting improvement and not a business improvement," said John Geraghty at North American Equity Services, a consulting firm.
He said that the market has been riding high based on the continued improvement of earnings, but "as future quarters go by, earnings comparisons will become tougher and tougher to beat."
Among other indexes, the Nasdaq Composite index closed up 8.47 points Friday at a record of 1,349.05 and for the week, it gained 17.03.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 6.42 to a record of 776.17. For the week, it rose 16.67 points.
The American Stock Exchange index rose 2.59 to 589.95, capping a gain of 3.91 for the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks rose 3.19 to a new high of 409.31, and was up 8.55 from last Friday.
